tradition.lineage: Nuevo tango developed through Astor Piazzolla’s expansion of Argentine tango into composed concert music, incorporating jazz, counterpoint and adventurous harmony. It circulates through instrumental ensembles and published solo arrangements as well as recordings.

extras.description: Tango phrasing meets extended harmony, contrapuntal lines and dramatic contrasts. Concert works and intimate instrumental arrangements carry this repertoire beyond the conventions of the traditional dance orchestra.

tradition.name: Old School Hard Trance
tradition.lineage: Old school hard trance revisits the driving trance records of the 1990s and their continuing life in DJ sets, collector communities and revival releases. Noom and related European rave catalogues connect hard kicks, acid-tinged sequences and emphatic melodic hooks with the energy of early hard dance.

Long blends and breakdowns connect familiar records with renewed club energy, while archival mixing and record collecting keep the older repertoire in circulation alongside contemporary hard-dance selections.

tradition.name: Plena Uruguaya
tradition.lineage: Plena uruguaya developed within Uruguay’s tropical dance orchestras, adapting Caribbean influences into local rhythms, arrangements and repertoires. Montevideo ensembles, dance venues and later recordings carried the style across generations, alongside related cumbia and other national popular traditions.

extras.description: Voices and bright trumpet figures ride a piano-and-bass foundation, with timbales and hand drums shaping the dance pulse. Repeated phrases and clear rhythmic grounding link the orchestral sound to social dancing; later ensembles expand the palette with electronic keyboards and other horns.

All six families are retained, with multiples aggregated rather than silently dropped. Later roster on the same artist page includes trombone and additional singers; it is separate from the dated earlier practice, not denied. This is not the previously held twelve-family Kumbiaracha2024 recording. Bass source subtype is unspecified; fretted electric bass is authored. Standard upright piano, open Bb ensemble trumpets, steel stick timbales and oak/mule-hide conga construction are editable representative choices, not measured original gear. Source rhythm is Uruguayan plena’s dance-orchestra adaptation; existing son-context paila-pattern supplies shared foundational technique, not a claim of exclusively Cuban son. The direct national teacher lists timbales across Plena Uruguaya and related repertories. The broader recorded repertoire includes many lighter popular arrangements.
